newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bonds rally at close, yields seen pushing lower.
newsitem.headline: NZ bonds rally at close, yields seen pushing lower.

* NZ bonds maintain strong underlying tone at close
* Bills sell slightly while futures rally
* U.S. election reaction seen driving NZ in short term
New Zealand bonds finished in fine form on Wednesday after a strong performance.

Dealers said there had been reasonable buying through the mid curve overnight, and also some in the longer end from offshore. Mid bonds were boosted by a NZ$100 million three-year eurokiwi issued overnight by Walt Disney. The 02/00 maturity rallied seven points to 7.0 percent.

Dealers said local bonds were helped by a bullish close in U.S. Treasuries ahead of the announcement of presidential election results. Incumbent Democrat president Bill Clinton soundly defeated Republican contender Bob Dole when the votes were counted on Tuesday evening (US time), and dealers expect good price action when U.S. markets re-open.

"We will definitely be dictated to by what is happening in the States. It is driving us definitely at the moment -- it has taken a bit of a grip on New Zealand and perhaps Australia too, to a lesser degree," one dealer said.
"It's looking like pushing a little bit lower," he said of local bond yields, adding that yields were also being helped by limited supply.
Trade died down in the afternoon after reasonable activity on the open.

The Australian market failed to have much impact on New Zealand despite a 50 basis point cut in official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 7.0 percent. The easing had been priced in for some time, and some analysts suggested there was slight disappointment the cut was not more aggressive.
Australian debt securities were mixed on profit-taking after the cut. The 90-day bank bills climbed six points and three year bonds climbed five, but the 10-year bond fell two.
"I think the Australian market was caught a little long on the rate cut, basically, but New Zealand was a slightly different beast on the day," one local dealer said.
Money market traders said the physical and futures markets had temporarily parted company, with 90-day bank bills selling off three basis points while the front futures contract rallied one point.
"It's a bit peculiar really -- the bill market is stuck in the mud and the synthetic market is still being driven by pretty strong offshore flows," one said.

"Cash is still being held up, and there is a lot of supply in the market with a lot of seasonal t-bills to pay for, the maturity of the 11/96 bonds and what-not. Then you've got these euros, and the synthetic people covering their risk in the futures market," he said.
